<reason>Both sides were competent and disciplined (honest A1:/A2: labeling, no fake sourcing, plausible background claims). PRO's core was strong and memorable — interest exceeding defense as a "receipt," sequencing, certainty of interest versus speculative returns — and PRO defended well by conceding the household analogy was only a device, distinguishing post-2010 European austerity from a pause on new commitments, and extending the rule symmetrically to unpaid-for tax cuts. But CON found and exploited the decisive vulnerability: PRO's own characterization of the plan as "a pause on addition, not a program of subtraction," which CON converted into a clean, repeatable test — does the rule reduce the very interest cost it treats as the reason to act? PRO answered honestly ("no clean ten-year number") but never showed the rule bites on the drivers CON identified (existing stock, rates, aging programs, revenue base), so the targeting-failure argument survived. CON also neutralized PRO's uncertainty asymmetry by pointing to symmetrically certain deferred costs and by offering an affirmative mechanism (case-by-case scoring, sunsets, pay-as-you-go, cut where the money is) plus an actual threshold when pressed — the exact demands PRO's pressure questions made. CON's best judo was turning PRO's concessions (bind tax cuts, burden on each proponent) into "that's ordinary budgeting, which the motion forbids." PRO's closing reply that "ordinary budgeting produced this problem" was the right instinct but arrived without showing measurable savings, leaving CON's central test unanswered. CON's clipped opening is a real but small execution cost, since the truncated line was developed later.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]-[B2.2] seizing on PRO's "pause on addition, not a program of subtraction" and reframing it as deficit maintenance that "purchases a receipt that goes down by roughly nothing," then locking it in with the pressure question demanding a ten-year savings figure — which PRO conceded it could not supply — and closing on "risk-aversion is only a reason to act if the action reduces the risk."</best_rebuttal>
